article.titel: How to Get Your Life Together: A Life Admin Checklist
article.h1: How to Get Your Life Together: A Life Admin Checklist
article.desc: Use a practical life admin checklist to sort loose ends, identify a real deadline, choose one next action, and build a review you can return to.
article.zoekterm: how to get your life together
article.antwoord: To get your life together, start by making your current obligations visible. Put loose ends in one place, separate actual deadlines from things you would simply like to improve, and choose one action you can carry out. The checklist below helps you organize everyday life admin without turning every unfinished task into a new project. Use paper or a note you already have.

secties.kop: 1. Define the problem in observable terms
alineas: The phrase get my life together can hide several different needs. An unanswered letter, a crowded calendar, a pile of laundry, and uncertainty about your career require different responses. Before adding a new routine, name the situation that prompted you to look for help today.

Write a sentence that someone else could understand without knowing your whole life: I cannot find the appointment details, or I have promised more work than I have room to complete. This gives you something you can check. Avoid using your list as a verdict on your character.

If the main question is whether to change direction, use our separate starting-over guide. This page is for organizing the obligations you already have and deciding what happens next. You can use it even while your longer-term plans remain uncertain.
lijst: The practical problem I need to address is _____.
I will recognize a useful improvement when _____.

secties.kop: 2. Collect loose ends in one place
alineas: Choose one page or note and list the things you are trying to remember. Include messages you need to answer, dates to check, household tasks, paperwork, and commitments to other people. Keep this first pass brief enough to finish. You can add another item when you discover it.

Check the places where obligations actually arrive, such as your calendar, mail, and messages. Do not assume that remembering a task means you know its deadline or requirements. Mark missing information so that looking it up becomes a specific next action.

You do not need a new app or a carefully designed notebook. If you already keep a useful calendar, keep using it. The aim is to make the open items visible, not to move everything into a different system.
lijst: Home: What needs cleaning, replacing, arranging, or putting away?
Paperwork and appointments: What needs a reply, a date check, or a document?
Work or study: What have I agreed to deliver, and to whom?
People and care: Which messages, arrangements, or shared responsibilities need attention?

secties.kop: 3. Separate deadlines, next actions, and waiting
alineas: Read the list once and give each item a practical status. A task with a confirmed deadline belongs on your calendar with the information needed to act. An item waiting on another person needs a follow-up date. An idea you might pursue later can stay on a separate later list.

Check deadlines against the original notice or agreement. A task that feels uncomfortable is not automatically the most urgent one. If the consequences or instructions are unclear, the next action may be to ask the responsible organization for clarification.

Choose what to handle first from the facts you have: the real deadline, the consequence of delay, and the resources available. This checklist cannot decide every priority for you. It can help reveal which decision needs more information or another person's help.
lijst: Confirmed deadline: What is due, when, and where did I verify it?
Ready to act: What is the next visible action?
Waiting: Who or what am I waiting for, and when will I check again?
Later or remove: Can I defer, decline, or stop this commitment?

secties.kop: 4. Turn one item into a workable next action
alineas: Pick one item and replace its broad label with an action you can start. Sort out my paperwork could become find the latest letter and write its reference number on this page. Clean the house could become clear the kitchen counter. Choose the action because it advances the item you selected, not because it makes the list look impressive.

Include the material or information the action requires. If a form needs a document you cannot find, locating or requesting that document comes before finishing the form. A waiting status is more accurate than repeatedly putting an impossible task back on today's list.

Choose a realistic opportunity for the action. Specify where you will be and what you will have available. If the task needs more time than you have, record a smaller preparatory step or arrange an appropriate time instead of pretending it fits.
lijst: My next action is _____.
I need _____ before I can do it.
I will do it at _____, in _____, using _____.

secties.kop: 5. Copy this one-page life admin card
alineas: Use the following lines for your own situation. You can copy them into a notebook or document and print that document. This is a text worksheet, not a separate downloadable PDF or a checkout offer.

For example: Item: confirm an appointment. Verified date: Wednesday, from the confirmation message. Next action: reply with the requested information. Status: ready. Review: check for a response on Friday. The example is a format to adapt, not a recommended schedule for every appointment.
lijst: CONFIRMED DATE OR DEADLINE, IF ANY: _____.
WHERE I VERIFIED IT: _____.
NEXT ACTION: _____.
WHAT I NEED OR WHO CAN HELP: _____.
STATUS: ready / scheduled / waiting / later / removed.
NEXT REVIEW DATE: _____.

alineas: At your next review, record what happened to the selected item. Done, waiting on a reply, and needs a different approach are all useful observations. If the action was too large or the required information was missing, change the next step accordingly.

Keep the review short enough to repeat. You might attach it to an existing weekly calendar check, but choose a frequency that fits the obligations on your list. Time-sensitive matters may need earlier attention. Remove completed or abandoned items so they do not keep competing with current work.

The point is not to finish every item before you are allowed to feel organized. A useful record tells you what is current, what is waiting, and when you intend to look again. That record can still be helpful during a busy or difficult week.

secties.kop: 7. What the research supports, and what this checklist adds
alineas: Masicampo and Baumeister's 2011 experiments found that forming specific plans reduced interference from unfinished goals during other tasks. The study concerned particular experimental tasks and does not establish that a life admin checklist resolves every kind of overwhelm.

Harkin and colleagues' 2016 meta-analysis examined 138 studies of progress-monitoring interventions. On average, those interventions improved goal attainment. This supports checking progress as part of a plan, while leaving uncertainty about which method fits a particular person or situation.

The categories, card, examples, and sequence on this page are our editorial tools. The complete checklist has not been tested as an intervention. Use the parts that help you make decisions, and revise or leave out the parts that add unnecessary work.

A list of obligations and a repeated habit need different kinds of records. If this exercise identifies one action you want to practice regularly, the Lasting Change Workbook paperback is an optional way to keep that practice in a dedicated book. Check Amazon for the current listing and availability.

You can also continue with the page or notebook you already used. Buying a workbook is not required to complete the checklist. If you want to reconsider your direction before choosing a repeated action, read the seven-day starting-over guide next.

faq: Where should I start if every area feels disorganized?

Write down the concrete problem that needs attention first, then check whether it has a real deadline or consequence. Choose one action that fits your current resources. Keep the remaining items on the page so you do not need to decide on all of them immediately.
What if I do not know the deadline or the next step?

Mark the missing information instead of guessing. Your next action may be to find the original notice, check an agreement, or ask the relevant person what is required. Record where the answer came from.
How is this different from the seven-day reset plan?

This checklist organizes existing obligations and follow-ups. The seven-day reset plan helps you explore what to keep or change in your life. You can use the checklist without changing your direction or committing to a seven-day sequence.
Do I need an app or a paid planner?
No. A page, a note, and your existing calendar are enough to use this structure. A dedicated book is optional if you decide it would help you record a repeated practice.
How can I tell whether my system is helping?

Check whether you can identify the next action and locate the information you need. At review time, record what changed and what remains blocked. A longer list or a more attractive planner is not, by itself, evidence that your obligations are easier to manage.
